newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico Cetes rates down on calm, money mart change.
newsitem.headline: Mexico Cetes rates down on calm, money mart change.

text.p: Mexico's primary Cetes rates fell more than expected across the yield curve on Tuesday, with the one-month treasury bill leading the decline, analysts said.
Investors were cheered by a relative calm in Mexican financial markets and by moves by the central bank to increase liquidity by changing how it operates in the money markets, analysts said.
"It was a decline much more than expected in the market, and it reflects a little more calm in the economy at the moment," ING Barings economist Sergio Martin told Reuters.
Banco Union economist Ricardo Vazquez said a combination of lower secondary money market rates, a stable exchange rate and high real returns on the Cetes all helped the primary rates to fall.
The rate on the 28-day Cetes fell a sharp 238 basis points to 20.23 percent at Banco de Mexico auction.

A survey of nine money market dealers conducted before the auction found expectations of a decline of 139 basis points to 21.22 percent on the 28-day Cetes. Rates were also seen falling at longer terms.
Analysts had speculated that rates would fall partially on the influence of a new approach by Banco de Mexico to change its methods of adjusting liquidity in the money market.
The central bank has moved to selling repurchase agreements and Cetes directly into the market instead of draining liquidity by its daily deposit auctions.
The central bank has faced large flows of dollars into Mexico and higher interest rates than it might otherwise have wanted as a result of its effort to sterilize those inflows.
It also has increased the limit on the amount commercial banks can be short in their accounts with Banco de Mexico.
Dealers in the secondary market said on Tuesday they believed the shift in the central bank methods had boosted liquidity.
The declining rates may also be reflected in a weaker peso, analysts said.
"Lower yields may cause some weakness to be reflected in the peso," Valores Finamex economist Ann Ginsburg said in a report released before the auction.
"This would likely be viewed as constructive by both Banco de Mexico and market participants, however, given the peso's real appreciation so far this year," Ginsburg wrote.
Demand for the Cetes soared this week as well, rising to an extremely strong 19.02 billion pesos on the 3.0 billion pesos on offer.
The bid-to-cover ratio on the auction was 6.34, with the strongest demand seen in the 28-day and 91-day paper, which had bid-to-cover ratios of 7.24 and 8.33, respectively.
